46 maunds of hilsa caught in a single net, sold for nearly Tk 5m
item.description:
A fishing trawler has caught 46 maunds of hilsa in a single net in the Bay of Bengal near Kuakata in Patuakhali.

The fish were sold at Mahipur Fishery Port on Friday for approximately Tk 4.85 million (Tk 48.5 lakh).

The unusually large catch has brought renewed excitement among fishermen in the coastal area after a prolonged period of poor catches.

Alamgir Majhi, the owner of the fishing trawler FB Junaid, was on board when the fish were caught. He said the trawler caught 46 maunds of hilsa on Thursday near the last buoy of Payra Sea Port.

The trawler, loaded with hilsa, reached Mahipur Fishery Port at noon on Friday. The fish were then sold through an auction at a wholesale fish outlet called Manowara Fish.

“It has been nearly five years since I got such a large consignment of hilsa at once. This is great news. Catching 2,200 hilsa in a single net is no small thing. We have suffered losses for a long time, and with such a big catch, we hope to recover some of those losses, ” said Alamgir Hossain, owner of FB Junaid.

Sagir Akon, manager of Manowara Fish, said 24 maunds of the catch consisted of hilsa weighing 1kg or more. They bought those fish at Tk 115,000 per maund, equivalent to Tk 2,875 per kg. The 24 maunds therefore cost Tk 2.76 million.

The remaining 22 maunds consisted of hilsa weighing between 800 and 900 grams. Those were purchased at Tk 95,000 per maund, or Tk 2,375 per kg, bringing the total cost to Tk 2.09 million.

The entire 46-maund catch was therefore purchased for Tk 4.85 million.
Sagir Akon said hilsa prices this year were significantly higher than last year.

“Hilsa prices are very high in the market, so the fishermen who caught these 46 maunds received a good price,” he said.

Apu Saha, senior fisheries officer, Kalapara upazila, said,  “There has been a shortage of hilsa in the sea for quite some time. However, fishermen are still catching varying amounts of hilsa. If the rainfall continues, the catch is likely to increase further.”

Hilsa catches in the sea have declined compared with previous years, with overall production also falling. This has put pressure on fishermen’s livelihoods.

Mohammad Bakhtiar Rahman, a research assistant with the Healthy Ocean project implemented by WCS and WorldFish with funding from the Blue Action Fund, described the large catch as encouraging news for fishermen.

According to Bakhtiar, the catch could give hope to fishermen who spend days and nights at sea. However, he cautioned that such a large catch in a single day should not be considered an indicator of an overall abundance of hilsa.

He said the situation could be properly assessed later through continued monitoring and scientific data on fish availability.

He also stressed that maintaining the positive trend would require greater awareness among fishermen, avoiding fishing during the breeding season and ensuring the continued implementation of conservation measures.

Apu Saha, senior fisheries officer of Kalapara upazila, told Prothom Alo that hilsa availability in the sea had been declining for some time. However, fishermen were still catching hilsa in varying quantities.

“If the rainfall continues, more hilsa will be caught,” he said. “The greater the volume of hilsa caught, the more fishermen, fish traders and others involved in the hilsa trade will benefit.”

item.title: Iran says deal on Strait of Hormuz is close but not enough to open the waterway
item.description:
SAUDI ARAMCO-RESULTS/

Iran said on Saturday that a deal with Oman on control of the Strait of Hormuz was close but would not be enough to free up the waterway, and the United Arab Emirates said Iran had hit another ship there.

Agreement between Iran and Oman over the strait is seen as vital to a wider deal to end the war that began with US and Israeli attacks on Iran on 28 February and led to Tehran establishing a chokehold over the major energy export route.

A US official, who declined to be identified, had said on Friday that Washington anticipated an agreement soon between Iran and Oman, which sit on either side of the strait, so that normal oil traffic could resume.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said Iran and Oman were "very close" to agreement on a new shipping route through the strait but that reopening it depended on other conditions, including US compensation to Iran.

The secretary of Iran's top national security body, Mohammad Baqer Zolqadr, listed other demands including ending US threats against Iran, stopping aggression against Iran and its Lebanese, Palestinian, Yemeni and Iraqi allies, lifting a blockade and sanctions on Iran and freeing Iranian assets.

US hopeful Hormuz strait deal will be done “today or tomorrow”

Oman Reports Positive Negotiations, Condemns Ship Attacks

Oman condemned what it described as repeated attacks on vessels while transiting the strait, without assigning blame, and said that negotiations with Iran on arrangements for shipping through Hormuz were "positive and constructive".

"Oman stresses the importance of avoiding any actions that could affect these negotiations and the progress achieved in a manner that takes into account the interests of all parties," the foreign ministry said.

Araqchi said the previous shipping traffic separation scheme through the strait was no longer acceptable to Tehran and that Iran was discussing a temporary route with Oman while technical and legal issues surrounding a permanent route were resolved.

Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, a relative moderate, said he believed now was the best time for an agreement.

"There is cohesion, strength, and unity in the country, and as far as I know, Iran is considered victorious and powerful in this war," Iranian news agencies quoted him as saying.

Iran has responded to the US attacks by targeting US bases in Gulf states and Jordan as well as striking shipping in the narrow strait, which carried a fifth of the world's oil and gas shipments before the war.

The UAE said on Saturday that Iran had attacked a carrier affiliated with its state oil company with a missile as it transited the Strait of Hormuz, with no injuries reported, in the latest escalation in attacks on shipping there. The UK maritime trade monitor UKMTO said a vessel had caught fire after being hit by an unknown projectile but the fire was put out and there was no reported environmental impact.

US used “virtually all” of its long-range missiles during Iran war

There was no immediate comment from Iranian authorities.

In recent weeks, the Trump administration has repeatedly signaled that a deal to open the strait could be close, only to have Iran deny that talks are under way. It was unclear whether the latest flurry of negotiations would yield a more lasting arrangement.

"Once the deal is announced to restore commercial shipping without impediments, the United States will lift the blockade of Iranian ports," the US official told Reuters on Friday. US actions would be tied to Iran's implementation of its commitments, he said.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards, who have targeted the ships, also said on Saturday that reopening the Strait of Hormuz depended on Washington accepting Iran's conditions and was not related to the Iran-Oman negotiations.

"Whenever the United States accepts Iran’s conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will certainly be reopened," said Guards spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi, according to Iran's Tasnim news agency.

Sources Said This Week a Deal Would Give Iran Some Control

A proposed deal between Iran and Oman to help end five months of war between Iran and the US would give Tehran control over ships entering the Gulf through the strait, a senior Iranian source and two regional officials told Reuters on Wednesday, one of the biggest concessions yet to Iran.

US officials have repeatedly said they would never agree to Iran controlling access to the world's most important trade route for energy supplies. It was not clear whether they had sought to change the parameters of the deal.

Iran has used the hostilities to justify charging a toll on oil tankers. That, and the firing on ships that attempt to cross the strait without its permission, has badly disrupted global shipments, causing energy prices to surge and fueling inflation.

item.title: Tarique Rahman was tortured at JIC during 1/11: ICT chief prosecutor
item.description:
Chief Prosecutor of the International Crimes Tribunal (ICT) Md Aminul Islam today, Saturday said witnesses in different cases have testified that incumbent Prime Minister Tarique Rahman was tortured at the Joint Interrogation Cell (JIC) at the Directorate General of Forces Intelligence (DGFI) headquarters in Dhaka during the 1/11 period.

"The JIC that we visited today was the place where the Prime Minister Tarique Rahman was brought to one of its rooms during the 1/11 period. We have also found information through the accounts of various witnesses during our investigation that he was subjected to torture there. These findings will be reflected in the trials in due course," he said while talking to newsmen at the DGFI headquarters after inspecting the JIC this noon.

Terming today's visit as part of the trial proceedings, the chief prosecutor said, people were brought to this facility, detained and subjected to torture and other forms of abuse.

"It later became known as 'Aynaghar'. Detainees were held there in inhumane conditions for days, months and even years. We were able to get some sense of the brutality they endured through today's visit," he added.

Md Aminul Islam said they will urge the government to ensure that no TFI (Task Force for Interrogation) cell, JIC or so-called 'Aynaghar' is ever established again in Bangladesh in the future.

"If any citizen of the country commits a crime, he or she must be brought under the law and made to face trial. But no citizen should ever become a victim of any extrajudicial killing. No one should be subjected to unnecessary harassment by any law enforcement agency. No one should be detained and subjected to harassment in custody for days or months," he further said.

Led by ICT-1 Chairman Justice Golam Mortuza Mazumder, the delegation that inspected the JIC included Justice Shafiul Alam Mahmud and Justice Mohitul Haque Enam Chowdhury, Daily Manabzamin Editor Matiur Rahman Chowdhury, Supreme Court Reporters Forum General Secretary Mehedi Hasan Dalim, its Executive Committee Member Mazharul Hoque Manna, and Law Reporters Forum President Md Yasin, among others.

item.title: Why intellectuals become collaborators of autocracy
item.description:
Altaf Hossain was originally from Sylhet but was a staunch supporter of Pakistan. During the regime of military dictator Ayub Khan, his responsibility as the editor of the Dawn newspaper was to turn Bengalis into Pakistanis and Muslims. He was so successful in this task that Ayub gave him a place in his cabinet.

Altaf Hossain was not alone. Since the creation of Pakistan in 1947 and Bangladesh's independence in 1971, we have rarely experienced true democracy. Most of the time has passed under authoritarian regimes. During this long period, a section of Bengali intellectuals have stood by autocratic and semi-autocratic governments for one excuse or another. Some in the name of religion, some in the name of anti-Indianism, some in the name of the spirit of the liberation war, and some in the name of secularism and development have found justifications for siding with despotism.

Fall of Sheikh Hasina and lessons from history

We can also mention Syed Sajjad Hossain, who, despite witnessing the massacre of 1971, accepted it in the name of maintaining Pakistan's territorial integrity. Shortly after the Pakistani army launched a brutal attack on Dhaka University, he was rewarded by Pakistani authorities with the position of Vice-Chancellor of the same university. He was so loyal to Pakistan that he viewed the emergence of Bangladesh as the ''fall'' of East Pakistan.

As intellectuals, they forgot that their primary duty as intellectuals was not to befriend power but to relentlessly challenge the centres of power. They did the opposite. It's easy to protest against the enemy's injustice, but standing against one's own side's injustice is the true test of an intellectual's integrity. In this critical test, Awami intellectuals of Bangladesh have utterly failed.

There was no need for him to openly celebrate the genocide. He developed a narrative to uphold Pakistan's ideals, which portrayed the army as maintaining national unity and the Bengali resistance as an Indian-instigated separatism. This way, all the atrocities were obscured by ideology.

Constructing Consent

I'm not suggesting that Bengali intellectuals have a monopoly on constructing narratives in support of autocracy. Throughout history, there have always been groups of intellectuals eager to justify ruthless and diabolical regimes.

Antonio Gramsci and George Orwell have explained this concept very clearly and straightforwardly. What we now refer to as ''manufacturing consent'', riding on Noam Chomsky's shoulders, was first exposed by Gramsci in his Prison Notebooks. According to Gramsci, everyone is an intellectual, whether a bricklayer or a pen-professor, as we all use our intellect in some form of work.

However, there is a group among intellectuals whose job is to advocate for power using ladders of opinion, belief, or ideology. Without the narratives they construct, it would be impossible for dictatorships to survive. For Stalin, Hitler, Ayub, or Hasina, these intellectuals are as essential as fuel is to a car.

When the state is unable to fulfill its fundamental responsibilities

The autocrat's weapon is the gun. The intellectual's weapon is their pen and language. British journalist and author George Orwell demonstrated how a group of intellectuals could use everyday language to prove even the ruthless dictators like Stalin or Hitler as indispensable.

One function of political language is to prove truth as falsehood and falsehood as truth. This task is best accomplished by the country's prominent intellectuals. They are popular and have acceptance among ordinary citizens. So when such an intellectual takes up the pen for a corrupt king, whether they are a poet, journalist, or actor, people listen to them attentively and place their trust in their words. Their advocacy not only spares lies but also cold-blooded disappearances and murders.

When intellectuals become followers of autocracy

In Bangladesh, some intellectuals have turned into supporters of Awami authoritarianism while offering uncompromising support for the values of the Liberation War based on their ideological foundation. Civil rights are violated in the country, voting rights are taken away, and freedom of speech is restricted. Like everyone else, they too have witnessed these violations firsthand. The only difference is that they have considered these violations necessary for ideological reasons, singing praises or remaining silent in their support.

When it comes to the values of the Liberation War, these intellectuals have prioritised three things—preservation of the history of 1971, opposition to fundamentalism, and secularism. These are important values, but the spirit of the Liberation War is not limited to these principles or ideals. The rule of law, an independent judiciary, voting rights, freedom of speech, and an egalitarian society are also part of this spirit.

All of these values have been violated from the very beginning of the Awami era. In the last sixteen years of Hasina's rule, these violations have multiplied a hundredfold, turning into a full-fledged autocratic system. Yet, the blind eyes of the Awami intellectuals remain blind.

We have seen many intellectuals who are unwavering about the history and values of 1971. Yet, they have almost unconditionally supported Hasina's autocracy. When elections were held without votes, many of them argued that there is no alternative to Sheikh Hasina for Bangladesh. They considered siding with Hasina their duty. Some argued that there is no alternative to Hasina for maintaining secularism.

We saw in July 2024, when students and innocent people were being killed like birds at the hands of the security forces, almost every vice-chancellor of the country's major universities went to Ganabhaban to express their support for the measures taken by Prime Minister Hasina against the students and the public.

Many have privately acknowledged that democracy has been downgraded in Hasina's hands, or that the measures taken to stay in power are repressive. Yet, these conscientious intellectuals have considered Hasina and the Awami regime as the sole safeguards of the Liberation War. It's not that they were unaware of the contradiction involved. But after repeating the mantra for years, they themselves became lackeys of the autocracy.

The responsibility of intellectuals is not to befriend power

During the Soviet era, there were many intellectuals and devoted communists who, despite being aware of Stalin's autocratic rule, did not renounce their support for it. They believed there was no alternative to Stalin for the victory of the socialist revolution. One of them was Nikolai Bukharin. He was hung by the neck at Stalin's hands.

The famous German philosopher Martin Heidegger can also be mentioned. He believed in the superiority of the German nation and thought there was no alternative to Hitler to establish this superiority in the world.

The similarity between their arguments and propositions and the stance of Bangladeshi intellectuals in support of Hasina's dictatorship is striking. Bukharin knew that Stalin's hands were stained with the blood of innocent people; yet, he could not dissociate the revolution from the party, or the party from its leader.

Heidegger elevated Hitler from the position of an ordinary political ruler to a personification of Germany's historical destiny. Similarly, in Bangladesh, these intellectuals helped create a unified moral entity by merging secularism, the Awami League, and Sheikh Hasina.

As intellectuals, they forgot that their primary duty as intellectuals was not to befriend power but to relentlessly challenge the centres of power. They did the opposite. It's easy to protest against the enemy's injustice, but standing against one's own side's injustice is the true test of an intellectual's integrity. In this critical test, Awami intellectuals of Bangladesh have utterly failed.

#Hasan Ferdous is an essayist and columnist.

BNP leader dies of snakebite, family alleges antivenom was withheld
item.description:
A BNP leader died after being bitten by a snake in Galachipa upazila of Patuakhali on Saturday, with his family alleging that he was referred to Patuakhali without being administered antivenom at the local health complex.
The deceased was identified as Zakir Hossain Mridha, 45, son of Fazlul Karim Mridha of Kalikapur village in Galachipa Sadar Union. He was the general secretary of Ward No 1 BNP in the union.
The incident occurred around 7:30am when Jakir was having tea at home. A snake bit him on a toe of his left foot. After spotting the snake, he informed his wife and family members quickly took him to Galachipa Upazila Health Complex.
According to the hospital register, Zakir was admitted at around 7:45am. His family alleged that he was referred to Patuakhali without being given antivenom or adequate treatment.
His elder brother and former union parishad member, Abdul Awad Mridha, alleged that no treatment was provided at the hospital.
“My brother might have survived if he had been given antivenom. We demand a proper investigation into why he was referred without receiving antivenom or necessary treatment,” he said.
Ambulance driver Md Jewel said Zakir was conscious when they left for Patuakhali and that there was no delay on the way. However, doctors at a Patuakhali hospital declared him dead upon arrival.
Explaining the decision not to administer antivenom, attending physician Jannatul Naim Tanha said zakir was brought to the hospital in critical condition, with very high blood pressure and heart rate.
“Considering the possibility of a cardiac problem, we consulted senior physicians and decided not to administer antivenom before referring him to Patuakhali,” she said.
Galachipa Upazila Health and Family Planning Officer Md Mezbah Uddin said the health complex had 40 vials of antivenom in stock but it was not administered because Zakir had breathing difficulties, high blood pressure and was in critical condition.
“Based on his initial symptoms, it was not possible to determine whether he had been bitten by a venomous snake. After consulting a senior consultant, the attending physician decided to refer him to Patuakhali for better treatment,” he said.
Mezbah added that the hospital would investigate any complaint from the family and take necessary action if needed.
Meanwhile, Zakir’s family and local residents have demanded an investigation into whether antivenom was required, whether the doctors’ decision was appropriate given his condition and why the medicine was not administered.
Abdul Qaiyum, director of Animal Lovers of Patuakhali, claimed that Zakir had symptoms consistent with a venomous snakebite and should have been kept at the hospital for treatment rather than being referred elsewhere.
He said breathing difficulties and a sensation of the throat closing can be symptoms of venomous snakebite and argued that emergency supportive care should have been provided if the patient’s breathing was failing.

item.title: ‘Fish sanctuaries to be expanded in haors as govt moves to scrap leasing system’
item.description:
The government is taking steps to establish more fish sanctuaries in haors and wetlands to increase the breeding and production of native freshwater fish, Fisheries and Livestock and Agriculture Minister Mohammed Aminur Rashid said on Saturday.
He also said initiatives are underway to replace the existing leasing system for water bodies with a new mechanism aimed at protecting the interests of local communities.
The minister made the remarks while talking to journalists after inspecting the venue of the inaugural ceremony of National Fisheries Week 2026 at Achmita George Institution Mini Stadium in Katiadi upazila of Kishoreganj.
He said Bangladesh once had abundant native fish in its haors, baors, rivers, canals and wetlands. However, the availability of freshwater fish has declined over time due to the use of pesticides and chemical fertilisers, destruction of fish habitats and the shrinking of natural sanctuaries.
To address the situation, the government plans to create safe habitats for fish in haors and wetlands, including large pits and deep water-bodies where fish can breed and be conserved, he said.
“If fish eggs and fry can be protected, fish production will naturally increase,” the minister said, adding that sanctuary-based conservation of native freshwater fish would be strengthened.
Asked about concerns over microplastics in fish, Aminur Rashid said it was not only a problem for Bangladesh but a global concern. Microplastics have also been detected in seawater and marine fish, he said.
Bangladesh will take necessary measures in line with international research and decisions on the issue, he said, adding that the Environment Ministry’s relevant initiatives would also be important.

item.title: Two-day secondary teacher training and digital learning program ends
item.description:
A two-day teacher training program for nearly 70 mathematics teachers and head teachers from 21 secondary schools across four upazilas in Panchagarh ended on Saturday.
Jointly organized by Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education (DSHE), SAJIDA Foundation, and Kazi Farms Group, the workshop titled "Khan Academy Bangladesh Masterclass" and the closing ceremony were held at Eco Mahananda Cottage in Tetulia and attended by participating secondary school teachers, head teachers, and senior government officials.
Participating mathematics teachers received hands-on practical training on using classroom technology to make math learning accessible and engaging through the 'Khan Academy Bangladesh' platform. Additionally, head teachers gained detailed insights into utilising the platform's monitoring dashboard to observe school-level progress and performance. Alongside training, technical repair support is being provided to ensure functional digital equipment across participating schools.
At the closing ceremony, Chief Guest Nahida Parvin, Deputy Director (Research & Innovation Section, DSHE), stated: "As a mathematics student and educator myself, I deeply understand the necessity of math. Math is a subject where one concept cannot be understood without grasping its prerequisites; therefore, learning with conceptual understanding is crucial."
She further noted: "The government and all stakeholders are committed to ensuring quality education. I extend special thanks to the organizers for bringing such innovative projects to remote areas like Panchagarh. Our primary objective should be to spread development to peripheral regions across the country, rather than focusing solely on Dhaka."
Azwa Nayeem, CEO of Khan Academy Bangladesh, delivered the welcome address. She expressed gratitude to head teachers, teachers, and government officials, stating: "The Khan Academy platform plays a highly effective role in creating tech-supported classrooms. We seek everyone's full cooperation so that students, teachers, and head teachers can seamlessly use this platform to achieve math proficiency." She also extended sincere thanks to Kazi Farms for providing financial support to run operations in Panchagarh.
Attending the event, Md. Shariful Islam, Head Teacher of Bhojonpur Dimukhi High School, expressed his determination to track student progress via the dashboard to elevate all students to the 'Mastered' or proficient level in math.
Kazi Zeeshan Hasan, Director of Kazi Farms Group, stated in his speech: "Alongside business, Kazi Farms aims to create a positive impact on society through education. As we have multiple business operations in Panchagarh, we are delighted to contribute to the expansion of quality education in this remote and peripheral region of the country."
Among others, Jeshan Ahmed, Research Officer (Planning & Development Division, DSHE), Khairul Anam Md. Aftabur Rahman Helali (District Education Officer, Panchagarh), Ramizah Ahmed (Manager, Partnership & Fundraising Unit, SAJIDA Foundation), Khandaker Ahmed Ali (General Manager, Kazi Farms Limited), Upazila Secondary Education Officers, and other local administrative officials were present at the event.
With financial and technical support from SAJIDA Foundation and Kazi Farms, and with approval from DSHE, 'Khan Academy Bangladesh' is currently running its operations across 100 secondary schools in 7 districts -- Dhaka, Cumilla, Narayanganj, Gazipur, Narsingdi, Chandpur, and Panchagarh.

Dhaka-Sylhet Highway blocked over illegal sand extraction
item.description:
Residents of four villages in Ashuganj upazila of Brahmanbaria blocked the Dhaka-Sylhet highway for an hour on Saturday, protesting the illegal sand extraction from the Meghna River and its threat to nearby farmland and settlements.
Residents of Durgapur, Bahadurpur, Sohagpur and Tajpur blocked the highway by burning tyres at Bahadurpur from 11am to noon, triggering a five-kilometre traffic tailback and causing significant suffering for commuters and long-distance passengers.
The protesters alleged that sand is being extracted illegally from the Ashuganj section of the Meghna under the guise of a lease on the Bhairab side of Kishoreganj.
Rana Sikdar and Munabbir Billah, speaking on behalf of the protesters, said the large-scale extraction was accelerating river erosion and putting agricultural land in the surrounding villages at risk.
They also expressed concern over the possible disappearance of Sonampur, a centuries-old settlement that has emerged in the middle of the Meghna in Ashuganj.
The protesters claimed that local residents went to the river on Saturday to stop the sand extraction but were allegedly chased away by the extractors, some of whom were carrying weapons.
They subsequently formed a procession and blocked the highway, demanding the arrest and exemplary punishment of those involved in the illegal sand extraction.
Brahmanbaria reserved women’s seat MP Nadia Pathan Papon joined the protesters and expressed solidarity with their demands. She said she had spoken with the deputy commissioner and received assurances that sand extraction would be stopped within two days.
Papon also said that if anyone affiliated with the BNP was found involved in illegal sand extraction, action would be taken against them.
Following assurances from the authorities, the protesters withdrew the blockade at noon.
Ashuganj Upazila Nirbahi Officer Md Jamal Hossain, Assistant Commissioner (Land) Kazi Rabius Sarwar and Ashuganj police station Officer-in-Charge AKM Shafiqul Alam Chowdhury were present at the scene.
The officials assured the protesters that necessary action would be taken against illegal sand extraction.
Meanwhile, the highway blockade caused a five-kilometre-long traffic congestion stretching from Sohagpur bus stand to Bertala bus stand, leaving thousands of passengers and local commuters stranded.

item.title: RAB to become SRB
item.description:
The government’s plan to rename the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB) as the Special Response Battalion (SRB) includes proposed changes to its leadership, command structure, investigative powers, deputation rules and complaint mechanisms.
The nine-page draft law proposes changes to the existing legal framework, including eligibility for leading the force, the tenure of personnel deputed from other agencies, authority to order criminal investigations, and procedures for handling complaints and disciplinary matters.
At RAB’s 22nd founding anniversary on May 18, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said the government was not merely considering a change of name.
He said the government had taken an initiative to update RAB’s existing law to make it “up-to-date and world-class” while ensuring professionalism, transparency and accountability among its members. He also confirmed that changing the force’s name was under consideration.
The home minister said police account for 44% of RAB’s manpower, while another 44% come from the armed forces. The remaining personnel are from Ansar, Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) and civilian employees.
He said the government wanted to establish a modern and professional elite force while upholding human rights. He also said unlawful activities by individual officers could not be attributed to the entire institution.
The government is also considering US sanctions against RAB. Salahuddin said he hoped the United States would reconsider the sanctions if the force were reformed, reorganized or renamed under the new law.
RAB is currently part of the Armed Police Battalion. Under the existing law, a police DIG or an officer of equivalent rank from another disciplined force can be assigned responsibility for RAB’s direct control and supervision.
The 2003 amendment added four provisions — Sections 6A, 6B, 6C and 6D — specifically for RAB.
Under Section 7 of the proposed law, the government would appoint the SRB director general from among Additional IGP-level officers serving in Bangladesh Police.
Section 8 places the unit under the general control of the IGP and under the orders and overall supervision of the director general.
Members of the army, navy, air force and other disciplined forces could continue serving in SRB, but officers from those forces would no longer be eligible to become its director general if the draft remains unchanged.
Although the existing law allows officers from other forces to lead RAB, police officers holding the rank of Additional IGP have occupied the post in recent years.
AKM Shahidur Rahman was appointed RAB director general in 2024, followed by Ahsan Habib Palash this year.
RAB currently exists legally within the Armed Police Battalion.
Section 4 of the proposed law would establish SRB directly under Bangladesh Police as a specialized unit, with its headquarters in Dhaka.
Subject to government approval, subordinate units could also be established elsewhere in the country.
Personnel from multiple forces would continue to serve in the unit, while its legal identity and chain of command would be placed under Bangladesh Police.
The government has not proposed removing personnel from the army, navy, air force and other disciplined forces from the force.
The draft, however, introduces a minimum two-year service period for members posted, deputed or temporarily attached to SRB.
If there are sufficient grounds, the director general could recommend through the IGP that a member be returned to their parent force.
The multi-force structure would therefore remain, with a new legal requirement governing the duration of such postings.
Human rights activist Nur Khan Liton has objected to retaining personnel from multiple forces in the structure.
The draft also proposes changes to investigative authority.
Under the current framework, RAB can investigate crimes on government instructions. The 2003 amendment introduced separate provisions governing RAB investigations.
Section 15 of the draft states that a court, the government or the inspector general of police could direct the SRB director general to investigate a criminal offence.
The director general would then assign the investigation to a member holding at least the rank of sub-inspector.
The provision would allow courts, the government and the IGP to direct criminal investigations by SRB.
Section 10 lists SRB’s responsibilities, including maintaining internal security, collecting intelligence, recovering illegal arms, ammunition and explosives, and combating narcotics, cybercrime, human trafficking and organized crime.
The draft also specifically mentions action against violence against women and children, rape and trafficking.
Many of these responsibilities are already carried out by RAB.
Sections 12 and 13 provide powers to enter premises, conduct searches, seize items and make arrests in specified cases. They also allow SRB members, when necessary, to exercise the powers of police officers under the Code of Criminal Procedure.
Section 14 states that when an SRB member arrests a person or seizes evidence, the arrested person and evidence must be handed over or transferred immediately to the nearest police station in accordance with the Code of Criminal Procedure.
At the same time, Section 15 proposes that SRB maintain its own detention cells, evidence storage facilities and interrogation rooms for investigation purposes.
The draft does not specify separate time limits or detailed conditions for the use of the detention cells.
Section 22 proposes a five-member complaint redress committee to deal with complaints from citizens and allegations against SRB members.
The committee would include the SRB additional director general, a representative of the Home Ministry, an Additional IGP-level officer from Police Headquarters, the director of legal and media affairs, and a government-nominated person with at least 10 years of experience in human rights, law or judicial administration.
The committee would be able to investigate complaints, initiate inquiries when necessary and recommend action to the relevant authority if there is preliminary evidence supporting a complaint.
Nur Khan has questioned the independence of the proposed mechanism.
Speaking to Bangla Tribune, he said that although the name was changing, a large part of the old structure would remain.
“Under no circumstances is it right to create a security shield for citizens by involving members of the army, navy, air force or other forces in law enforcement agencies,” he said.
He also questioned whether the proposed complaint redress mechanism would be genuinely independent.
The draft lists several acts as disciplinary offences, including misconduct, abuse of power, following unlawful orders, torture and other wrongful conduct.
It also provides for preliminary inquiries and departmental action.
Until new rules are introduced, existing RAB court procedures and departmental proceedings could continue with necessary adaptations.
The draft also differs from the existing law on legal immunity. The existing law provides separate legal protection for actions carried out in “good faith” while performing official duties, while the nine-page SRB draft does not contain a similar standalone indemnity or immunity provision.
However, officials involved in the process said this should not be interpreted as meaning that all forms of legal protection would be removed.
The draft does not propose abolishing RAB and creating an entirely new force.
Under its repeal and savings provisions, RAB’s assets, rights, liabilities, records, contracts, ongoing activities, investigations and cases would continue under SRB.
Existing rules, orders and proceedings could also remain in force with necessary adaptations.
The proposal would retain much of RAB’s existing manpower and operational structure while changing its leadership, legal identity, investigative authority, deputation periods and complaint mechanisms.
The government says the new law is intended to make the force more professional, transparent and accountable.

item.title: 10 fruit shipments may have carried gold worth Tk300 crore
item.description:
A 16kg gold seizure from fruit crates at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport has led investigators to suspect that a much larger smuggling operation may have been running through the airport for at least a year, with fresh fruit imports allegedly being used as cover.
Investigators have found records of at least 10 fruit shipments imported from Hong Kong under the same company’s name over the past year. They now suspect that gold may have been smuggled through those shipments as well, potentially bringing around 250kg of gold into Bangladesh with an estimated market value of about Tk300 crore.
The latest findings have prompted law enforcement agencies to step up efforts to identify and arrest members of the alleged smuggling network.
Intelligence agencies, police and other law enforcement bodies are conducting operations in Dhaka and elsewhere as the investigation widens.
The investigation began after a shipment declared as fresh fruit was found to contain gold bars hidden inside specially constructed compartments in fruit crates at the airport’s Cargo Village.
Around 16kg of gold was recovered from the shipment.
Investigators believe the same technique may have been used in other consignments imported by the same company.
The documents showed no apparent discrepancies, allowing the consignments to pass through different stages of the cargo clearance process before reaching the release stage, according to investigation officials.
They suspect the operation exploited gaps in the international cargo system to bring gold into Bangladesh under the cover of legitimate fruit imports.
A second fruit shipment arrived in the same week as the seized consignment and was cleared without incident, according to sources familiar with the investigation.
Officials believe the seized shipment may therefore represent only a small part of a larger smuggling network.
Documents obtained during the investigation show a series of fruit consignments imported under the name of Food Link from Hong Kong.
16kg gold seizure exposes Tk300 crore smuggling route
Two shipments weighing 775kg and 742kg arrived in January 2025, while another weighing 696kg arrived in February.
Two more shipments, weighing 683kg and 688kg, arrived in March.
In July 2026, two separate consignments weighing 558kg and 636kg were imported.
Investigators have identified at least 10 shipments in total under the same importer’s name over the past year, with officials now rechecking each consignment.
Their preliminary assessment is that if the same quantity of gold recovered from the seized shipment had been concealed in the other consignments, the total value of the smuggled gold could be around Tk300 crore.
However, investigators have yet to establish that gold was actually carried in all of those shipments.
Customs raises concern over new route
Dhaka Customs House Additional Commissioner Mohammad Kamrul Islam said customs officials had so far identified five shipments linked to the investigation.
“We suspect the gold smuggling gang is now using the Hong Kong-Shahjalal Airport route as a new route,” he said.
He also pointed to a major limitation at the airport’s Cargo Village.
“There is no major scanner machine at the Cargo Village, so we cannot properly examine the consignments,” Kamrul said, adding that some of the current findings were based on assumptions.
“As a case has been filed, the actual facts will come out through the police investigation,” he said.
The investigation has also raised questions about the importer itself.
According to customs records, Food Link, listed at Plot-560, Manda, Uttarkhan, Dhaka-1230, was the registered importer of the consignments.
Its proprietor is identified as Md Golam Mostofa.
Investigators, however, found no office, warehouse or business operation at the registered address when they visited the location.
Officials involved in the preliminary investigation have consequently determined that the address appears to be fake.
The discovery has raised questions over how a company operating from a purportedly fictitious address managed to import multiple international consignments over an extended period and have them regularly cleared through the airport.
Investigators are also examining the role of those involved at different stages of the clearance process.
Another issue drawing attention is the role of the clearing and forwarding agent.
Documents related to the seized shipment show that A Razzak Trading was tagged in ASYCUDA World for clearance of the consignment.
Fasttrack Cargo Solutions Limited was listed as the master cargo agent, while Biman Bangladesh Airlines Limited was responsible for cargo handling.
Despite the investigation initially finding that the importer’s registered address was fake, the C&F agent involved in clearing the shipment has not been named as an accused in the case, raising further questions about the clearance process.
Sources in intelligence agencies and the customs department said Food Link had been regularly importing fruits from Hong Kong for a long period.
Investigators suspect the smugglers used specially designed concealed compartments inside fruit crates to transport gold bars while the accompanying documents declared only fruit.
The consignments reportedly arrived in Dhaka on cargo flights, including flights operated by Cathay Pacific Airways, from Hong Kong International Airport.
Investigators believe the network exploited weaknesses in the international cargo system to move gold through a route that appeared to be a legitimate commercial fruit-import channel.
The documents of the seized consignment show airway bill number 160-12740092.
The investigation is now focusing on the other consignments imported under Food Link’s name, as well as the individuals and agencies involved in their clearance.
The seized 16kg of gold may therefore prove to be only the visible part of a much larger operation.
Authorities are now working to determine whether the other shipments also carried gold and how the consignments were repeatedly cleared despite questions over the importer’s identity and address.

item.title: Dhaka bears brunt of dengue as peak may still lie ahead
item.description:
Dhaka is bearing the brunt of the dengue outbreak, with the highest number of infections and deaths recorded in the capital division, while experts warn that the worst of this year’s transmission may still be ahead.
Dengue infections could continue to rise throughout August and may reach their highest level in September, according to entomologist Dr Kabirul Bashar, raising concerns over a potentially prolonged outbreak.
The latest data from the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) shows that 18,673 people have been infected with dengue across the country this year, with 59 deaths reported so far.
Dhaka Division accounts for 6,871 of those infections — the highest among all divisions. Dhaka city alone has recorded 4,639 cases.
The division has also recorded the highest number of deaths, with 26 fatalities, 25 of them among residents of Dhaka city.
Dr Kabirul Bashar, professor of zoology and an entomologist at Jahangirnagar University, said the upward trend in dengue infections could continue through August.
However, he cautioned against assuming that August would mark the peak of this year’s outbreak.
“Depending on the situation, an upward trend in infections could also be seen in September,” he said.
Bashar urged authorities to treat both August and September as critical months for dengue control, rather than assuming that the threat will ease after August.
He said destroying Aedes mosquito breeding grounds should be the top priority.
Water should not be allowed to accumulate in homes, construction sites or surrounding areas, he said. Drums, buckets and other containers holding stagnant water should be cleaned regularly and kept overturned.
He also stressed the need to keep drains functional and maintain regular surveillance of construction sites, where stagnant water can create breeding grounds for Aedes mosquitoes.
If the environment that allows mosquitoes to breed can be changed, the spread of Aedes can be significantly reduced, he said.
Dhaka’s high population density, year-round breeding opportunities for Aedes mosquitoes and weaknesses in mosquito-control activities are among the main factors contributing to its heightened dengue risk, experts say.
Aedes mosquitoes are breeding in stagnant water in densely populated neighbourhoods as well as around homes and buildings under construction.
The scale of the problem means that mosquito-control campaigns limited to the rainy season are unlikely to be enough, experts said.
After Dhaka’s 6,871 cases, Barisal Division has reported 3,740 infections, followed by Chittagong with 3,228 and Khulna with 2,401.
Mymensingh has recorded 821 cases, Rajshahi 713, Rangpur 426 and Sylhet 111.
In terms of deaths, Khulna follows Dhaka with 10 fatalities. Barisal has recorded seven deaths, Mymensingh six, Chittagong five, Rajshahi three, and Rangpur and Sylhet one each.
Public health expert Dr Mushtak Hossain said dengue transmission tends to increase in densely populated areas as mosquito density rises.
He stressed the need to further decentralize healthcare services to ensure that dengue patients can be diagnosed and treated promptly.
“Necessary manpower and diagnostic facilities must be ensured at the grassroots level,” he said.
According to Hossain, extending dengue testing facilities to the union level would make disease detection and treatment more effective.
Experts also called for a shift away from isolated mosquito-control operations in individual areas towards a coordinated nationwide strategy.
They said places where stagnant water allows mosquitoes to breed must be identified and monitored regularly.
Where breeding sites cannot be completely eliminated, long-lasting insecticides or other effective measures to prevent mosquito breeding should be used, they recommended.
Experts have also called for a stronger role for local government institutions, particularly ward-level elected representatives and relevant authorities, in regular mosquito-control operations.
They warned that temporary campaigns during the dengue season cannot control the disease in the long term.
Instead, breeding sites need to be destroyed throughout the year, surveillance must be maintained regularly and mosquito-control activities must be coordinated centrally.
With Dhaka already accounting for the largest share of infections and deaths, and the possibility of peak transmission still ahead, experts say the coming two months will be critical in determining the trajectory of this year’s dengue outbreak.

item.title: Steady hands, clear paths: Supriya Kumar Chakraborty’s three decades of student guidance
item.description:
In the territory of education consultancy, few names appear to stand out in Bangladesh as much as Supriya Kumar Chakraborty’s.
Chakraborty started his career more than three decades ago, when he began working as a professional education counselor, immigration adviser, and tour manager.
Today, he is the founder and chief executive of SA Associates. He is known for advising every student to apply to institutes with honest intentions, those that do not ask for any unrealistic promises to be fulfilled.
The career of Supriya Kumar Chakraborty has a prolific history. In 1993, he started working at the Embassy of the Russian Federation in Bangladesh, where he served as a chief education officer for twelve years.
During this time, he was able to gain extensive knowledge of the educational field, studying the intricacies of the students’ placement process, as well as mastering the art of communication.
When Chakraborty left the Russian Embassy, he moved to Canada as a skilled worker. However, he did not give up on his ambitions of helping young Bangladeshis get access to education abroad.
In 2006, he opened an organization named SA Associates, which offered professional consultancy services to students and their parents.
Since then, it has gathered valuable experience in the spheres of education, emigration, and immigration. Today, SA Associates’ consultants provide assistance to those wishing to study in Canada, the UK, the US, Australia, and many other countries.
Chakraborty has had the opportunity to visit more than forty countries around the world, where he has participated in numerous conferences and meetings.
In addition, he has greatly contributed to his own professional development by taking various courses on education management, digital marketing, international education, and tourism.
Those who have worked with Chakraborty describe him as a person who always puts the client’s interests first.
He is known for his ability to analyze the student’s needs in terms of real possibilities.
Even now, he often shares his knowledge with his team of young specialists, reminding them that quality processing of documents, honest intentions, and a well-laid plan are the pillars of a successful application.
Chakraborty is known to his colleagues for being a mentor who understands the importance of developing his team.
Perhaps, one of the most important lessons that Chakraborty has learned throughout his professional journey is that a successful education consultancy service should strive to provide quality assistance to the clients.
To him, this philosophy serves as the absolute priority, as well as the primary mission of his own organization.
In his practice, Chakraborty has had to reject many opportunities, including those that seemed highly lucrative at the time.
He believes that in order for an education consultancy to truly be successful, it should have a good reputation among students for providing honest and reliable services.
Therefore, he focuses on working only with those applicants whose intentions are sincere and who understand the importance of the documents they submit.
In many ways, the success of an education consultancy now depends on how successfully it updates with the changing world. Immigration policies, the entry of new players into the market, as well as rapid digitalization; all of this requires organizations to be constantly aware of innovations.
Chakraborty is known to pay great attention to new trends and developments in the field of education consultancy.
He always emphasizes that there is a big difference between giving orders to people and inspiring them to achieve a common goal.
This approach has allowed him to establish long-term, trusting relationships with many students and their parents.
As for Chakraborty’s own vision, it is focused on encouraging young people to gain quality knowledge.
He believes that SA Associates can and should move forward and become even more successful. However, he always returns to the idea that the applicant’s dream should not be bigger than his real capabilities.
To his mind, the reputation of an honest and trustworthy expert is paramount.
Therefore, he will never sacrifice the interests of the client in favor of fulfilling the task given to the company.
He believes that it is this idea that should be at the heart of any education consultancy.
After all, it is not just a business, but also a chance to help every young person achieve their dreams.

PM urges UNOs to serve people with responsibility, humanity
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Saturday urged Upazila Nirbahi Officers (UNOs) to work with the highest sense of responsibility and humanity for the development of the country and welfare of its people, saying public service is a major trust and blessing for those entrusted with state responsibilities.
“Today we are here, tomorrow we will not be. Let us all try to leave a safe Bangladesh for the next generation, where everyone can live a little better,” he said. The prime minister is speaking at a meeting with UNOs from different upazilas at his office in Tejgaon, said a release issued by the PM’s Press Wing.
Describing field-level officials as a bridge between the government and the people, he said an upazila where an UNO is posted may not be his or her own, but it is still a part of Bangladesh and its people should be treated like their own. “If we want to put this small country in order, we all have to work together,” he said.
Tarique Rahman also urged the UNOs to play a more active role in raising public awareness, saying every social problem cannot be solved simply by making or enforcing laws.
He stressed the need for stronger local initiatives to protect the environment.
The prime minister noted that Dhaka has long remained among the world’s most polluted cities, but said recent improvements are a positive sign that should be built upon.
He urged UNOs to encourage people and local authorities to plant more trees. “If officials motivate people who already want to plant trees, an individual who plants 10 trees could be encouraged to plant 50.”
Tarique Rahman also asked the field administrators to promote sports at the local level, saying sports help young people develop discipline and positive habits. He said sports events need not be limited to national occasions such as Victory Day or Independence Day and could be organised around any meaningful local occasion.
The prime minister expressed concern over what he described as a decline in compassion and humanitarian values in society.
He suggested that UNOs visit schools and help raise children’s awareness about humanity, compassion and care for animals and nature. He said such values, once taught through family, society and religious practices, have weakened over time.
Tarique Rahman said efforts are being made to bring them back, including by incorporating lessons on humanity and compassion for animals at the primary level.
At the meeting, he praised and thanked UNOs from 83 upazilas for completing canal re-excavation projects and returning surplus funds to the government treasury.
During the meeting, UNOs shared the impact of canal re-excavation projects in their respective upazilas, particularly on agriculture, water management and people's daily lives.
They said areas that previously produced two crops a year are now producing three crops following the re-excavation of canals.
Improved drainage and irrigation have also brought positive changes to farming and local water management, the UNOs said.
They also conveyed messages of thanks and gratitude from beneficiaries to the Prime Minister.
Receiving the messages, he said the main objective of re-excavating canals is to restore the traditional riverine character of Bangladesh.
Tarique Rahman warned that the country’s groundwater level is gradually falling, which could create a serious crisis in the future. “We have to prepare from now to face that situation,” he said.
He said the government plans to re-excavate 20,000 kilometres of canals across the country in phases.
The prime minister expects the programme to bring long-term benefits by conserving water, increasing agricultural production, reducing waterlogging and maintaining environmental balance.
He said national development is not limited to infrastructure or economic growth; building humanity, compassion, and a sense of responsibility among people is also an important part of development. “Our main issue is one. Our goal and objective are also one,” he said.
